Cotswolds by Motorcycle: A Scenic Route

The Cotswolds offer a different kind of scenic riding — not dramatic mountains or wild coastline, but the gentle, rolling beauty of England's heart. Honey-coloured stone villages, flowing B-roads through green farmland, and a pace of life that invites you to slow down and savour every mile.

The Route (100 miles)

Start in Cheltenham and loop through the Cotswolds' finest villages: Bourton-on-the-Water, Stow-on-the-Wold, Chipping Campden, Broadway, and back via Winchcombe and Sudeley Castle.

Key Villages and Stops

  • Bourton-on-the-Water: The Venice of the Cotswolds, with the River Windrush flowing through the village green. Busy in summer but undeniably beautiful.
  • Stow-on-the-Wold: A hilltop market town with antique shops and a commanding position overlooking the surrounding countryside.
  • Chipping Campden: Perhaps the most beautiful High Street in England. Medieval wool merchants' houses in perfect Cotswold stone.
  • Broadway: A broad main street (hence the name) lined with galleries, tea rooms, and stone houses. Broadway Tower nearby gives panoramic views.
  • Bibury: Arlington Row — a line of 14th-century weavers' cottages — is the most photographed village scene in England.

The Roads

Cotswold riding is about flowing B-roads through rolling countryside. The roads follow the contours of the limestone hills — gentle climbs, sweeping descents, and long views across the Severn Vale. Speed isn't the point here — rhythm is.

  • The B4632 from Cheltenham to Broadway is particularly enjoyable — sweeping curves through open countryside.
  • The A44 from Broadway to Chipping Norton offers faster flowing riding with good views.
  • Minor roads between villages (follow signs, not satnav) reveal the quietest, most beautiful lanes.
The Cotswolds are busy with tourists in summer, especially weekends. Ride midweek or in shoulder season for the best experience. Spring (bluebells in the woodlands) and autumn (golden light on stone villages) are the most photogenic seasons.

Food and Drink

The Cotswolds excel at gastronomy. Highlight stops include:

  • Pubs serving local ales and hearty food in almost every village
  • Farm shops selling local cheese, meat, and bread
  • The Chef's Dozen bakery in Stow-on-the-Wold
  • Afternoon tea at any number of tea rooms — this is that kind of landscape

Beyond the Tourist Trail

While the famous Cotswold villages are undeniably beautiful, the B-roads between them are where the riding magic lives. The lanes connecting Lower Slaughter to Upper Slaughter, or Naunton to Guiting Power, wind through hidden valleys with barely another vehicle in sight. These are single-track roads with grass growing up the middle in places — quintessential English country lanes.

The Cotswold escarpment along the western edge offers the most dramatic riding in the area. The road from Cheltenham to Broadway via Cleeve Hill climbs to 1,083 feet — the highest point in the Cotswolds — with panoramic views across the Severn Vale to the Welsh mountains beyond. On a clear day, the view extends over five counties.

For evening entertainment, the Cotswolds has more charming pubs per square mile than almost anywhere in England. The Slaughters Country Inn, the Wheatsheaf in Northleach, and the Wild Rabbit in Kingham are all excellent choices for a post-ride dinner in historic surroundings.

Biker Culture in the Peak

The Peak District has a strong biker culture thanks to its central location and excellent roads. Matlock Bath, the so-called 'Little Switzerland' on the banks of the River Derwent, is a traditional Sunday gathering point for bikers. The promenade fills with motorcycles on warm weekends, and the atmosphere is convivial and welcoming.

The Cat and Fiddle pub at the summit of the A537 was once the second-highest pub in England. Though currently undergoing redevelopment, the location remains a popular biker stop with expansive moorland views. The nearby Roaches — a dramatic gritstone escarpment — provides stunning views across the Staffordshire moorlands.

Edale, at the start of the Pennine Way, is worth a stop for walkers and riders alike. The village sits in a dramatic bowl beneath Kinder Scout and Mam Tor, and the short walk to the foot of Kinder Downfall gives a sense of the wild moorland that surrounds the Peak's riding roads.

The Dales also offer excellent food stops. Wensleydale Creamery in Hawes — home of Wallace and Gromit's favourite cheese — offers tours and tasting. The George and Dragon in Dent serves locally sourced food in a 17th-century coaching inn. And the Moorcock Inn at the junction of the B6259 and A684 has been serving travellers since the coaching era.

Planning Your Peak District Ride

The Peak District is easily accessible from most of England, making it perfect for day rides. From Manchester, the Snake Pass is 40 minutes away. From Sheffield, Stanage Edge and the Hope Valley are on the doorstep. From the Midlands, Dovedale and the Manifold Valley are within easy reach. Accommodation ranges from camping at Fieldhead in Edale to boutique B&Bs in Bakewell and Buxton. The market town of Bakewell is a natural stop — the original Bakewell pudding from the Old Original Bakewell Pudding Shop is a mandatory touring treat. Castleton, at the foot of Mam Tor, is an atmospheric village with show caves, a castle ruin, and several good pubs that welcome muddy-booted bikers arriving from the passes above.

The Yorkshire Dales are ideally suited to long weekend touring. Base yourself in Hawes (central, good facilities) or Settle (southern, railway connections) and explore by day ride. The national park has excellent visitor centres at Malham, Hawes, and Reeth with maps, weather information, and local knowledge. Fuel is available in Hawes, Settle, Kirkby Stephen, Richmond, and Skipton — plan your route through these towns. Read our Cotswolds Motorcycle Destination Guide: England's Golden Hills guide for more.
keyTakeaways: This 100-mile loop from Cheltenham links Bourton-on-the-Water, Stow-on-the-Wold, Chipping Campden, Broadway and Winchcombe.
Cotswold riding is about rhythm not speed, flowing B-roads through rolling limestone countryside.
Cleeve Hill on the Cheltenham to Broadway road reaches 1,083 feet, the highest point in the Cotswolds, with views over five counties.
The lanes between villages, such as Lower to Upper Slaughter, are quiet single-track where the real magic lives.
Ride midweek or in shoulder season; spring bluebells and autumn's golden light on stone are the most photogenic.

faq.q: Is the Cotswolds good for fast riding?
faq.a: No, and that is the point. Cotswold riding is about rhythm rather than speed, on flowing B-roads that follow the contours of the limestone hills with gentle climbs, sweeping descents and long views across the Severn Vale. Rushing spoils the experience and the many villages have low limits. Settle into an unhurried pace and enjoy the quintessential rolling English scenery.

The B-roads and single-track lanes between the famous villages are where the riding magic lives. The lanes connecting Lower Slaughter to Upper Slaughter, or Naunton to Guiting Power, wind through hidden valleys with barely another vehicle in sight, some with grass growing up the middle. The western escarpment road over Cleeve Hill is the most dramatic, climbing to 1,083 feet with views over five counties.

faq.q: When should I visit the Cotswolds?
faq.a: Ride midweek or in shoulder season, as the Cotswolds are busy with tourists in summer, especially at weekends. Spring brings bluebells in the woodlands and autumn brings golden light on the stone villages, making both the most photogenic seasons. The famous villages such as Bourton-on-the-Water and Bibury are best seen early in the day before the coach parties arrive.

faq.q: Where can I eat and stay?
faq.a: The Cotswolds excel at food, with pubs serving local ales and hearty food in almost every village, plus farm shops and tea rooms. The Chef's Dozen bakery in Stow-on-the-Wold is a good stop, and for dinner the Slaughters Country Inn, the Wheatsheaf in Northleach and the Wild Rabbit in Kingham are all excellent in historic surroundings. Book accommodation ahead in peak season.
